html:
Muhammad bin Tughluq was sultan of Delhi from 1325 to 1351. Under him the Delhi Sultanate reached its widest extent and then began to break up. He was learned in philosophy, medicine and Persian verse, and his bold plans failed one after another.

  • The capital: in 1327 he ordered the court and many of Delhi's people to move 1,100 kilometres south to Daulatabad, to hold the Deccan. Many died on the road. He let them return some years later.
  • The coins: about 1330 he issued copper and brass tokens to pass at the value of silver, an idea taken from Chinese paper money. People forged them at home, and he had to buy them all back with real silver.
  • The taxes: he raised the land tax between the Ganges and the Yamuna just as a famine began, and the farmers fled.

Ibn Battuta served him as a judge for about eight years and left a sharp portrait: a ruler whose gate was never without a poor man made rich or a living man put to death (see his account).

Revolts followed. Madurai broke away in 1335, Bengal in 1338, Vijayanagara rose in 1336 and the Bahmani Sultanate in 1347. He died in Sindh chasing a rebel.
